panels.description: Meera's room by day. Meera, surprised, holding her phone. Email on screen from BazaarBox.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Flat 4B? I moved out of there months ago.

panels.description: Phone screen: a social media ad from AdNest.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: And now some company called AdNest knows what I bought?

panels.description: Nyay floats up beside the phone.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Before you do anything, find out what BazaarBox actually holds about you, and who it shared it with.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: I haven't opened that app in a year. Shouldn't my data be gone by now?

options.label: Ask BazaarBox what data it holds about her
Complain to the Data Protection Board straight away

panels.description: Phone screen: unsubscribed confirmation.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Done. Easy.

panels.description: Next day. Another AdNest ad.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Seriously?

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Unsubscribing stops one kind of email. It doesn't tell you what BazaarBox holds, and it doesn't touch what it already shared.

panels.description: Phone screen: the Data Protection Board's online complaint form. Meera taps "No".
The form shows that she must first use the company's grievance redressal.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: So the Board won't even look at it?

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Not yet. The company gets the first chance to fix it. The Board is your next step if it doesn't.

panels.description: Phone screen: the BazaarBox app's footer.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Registered email… that's my old college one.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Companies have to publish how to make a request, and what details they need to know it's really you.

options.label: Sign in to the Privacy Centre with her old college email and request her data
Email privacy@bazaarbox.example from her new work email: "Send me my data."

panels.description: Meera at her office desk. BazaarBox's reply.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: They're stalling!

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Actually, this is fair. They told you exactly how to ask, and checking it's really you protects your data too.

panels.description: Meera at her desk at home. Phone screen: BazaarBox data summary.
panels.caption: Two weeks later.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Three years of orders. And there's AdNest.

panels.description: Video call with Arjun.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: That's the point of asking. Now you know who else has your data, and what they got.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Can I get a copy to take to another shopping app?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Indian law doesn't give you that. You get a summary, not a portable copy.

panels.description: Phone screen: BazaarBox Privacy Centre, with two buttons.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: The address is wrong, and I don't shop there any more.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: You can ask them to fix what's wrong, and to erase what you no longer want them to keep.

options.label: Correct the address and erase her account and data

panels.description: Phone screen: BazaarBox's email.
panels.caption: Ten days later.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: So they don't have to delete everything?

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Not what another law says they must keep. And a good reply tells you what was kept, and why.

panels.description: Meera, neutral, rereading the email.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: And AdNest?

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: AdNest is a separate company with its own copy. That's a question for another day.

options.label: Complain to the Board that BazaarBox kept her invoices

panels.description: Meera starts typing a complaint. Nyay floats in front of the screen, worried.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Hold on. Keeping records a law requires isn't a breach. And the Act asks people not to file false or frivolous complaints.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Fair. They did what I asked.

panels.description: Phone screen: BazaarBox's email.
panels.caption: Ten days later.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: At least the deals will reach the right flat now.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Your address is fixed. But they still hold three years of your orders, and can keep using them as far as your consent allows.

panels.description: Office. Arjun at his desk, happy.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Here's something most people don't know. A shopping app with at least 2 crore users has to erase an inactive user's data after three years, and warn them 48 hours before.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: So if I'd just waited, it would have gone anyway?

panels.description: Nyay, neutral.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: Eventually. The three years run from your last visit, your last request, or the date that rule started applying, whichever is latest. For you, that's years away. And every request you make starts the clock again.

panels.description: Meera's room by day. Meera, happy, scrolling her phone.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Fewer kitchen ads already.

lines.speaker: nyay
lines.text: And next time an app asks for your data, you'll know what to ask back.

CS6.question: Myth or reality? "If I unsubscribe from a company's emails, it has to delete my data."
CS6.explanation: Unsubscribing only stops those emails. To find out what a company holds, or to have it erased, you have to ask it.

CS7.question: Before you complain to the Data Protection Board, you must first:
options: Use the company's own grievance process
CS7.explanation: The company gets the first chance to fix the problem. If it doesn't, you can go to the Board.

LS7.question: Can Meera complain to the Board before using BazaarBox's grievance mechanism?
LS7.modelAnswer: No. s. 13(3) requires a Data Principal to exhaust the opportunity of redressing her grievance with the Data Fiduciary before approaching the Board. Under s. 13(1) the fiduciary must provide readily available means of grievance redressal, and Rule 14(3) requires it to publish a response period not exceeding 90 days.

LS8.question: BazaarBox tells Meera to use its Privacy Centre with her registered email. Is it obstructing her rights?
LS8.modelAnswer: No. Rule 14(1) requires the fiduciary to publish the means for making rights requests and any particulars, such as a username or other identifier, needed to identify her. Rule 14(2) lets her make the request using those means and particulars. Its reply also names the Grievance Officer, as Rule 9 requires in every response to a rights request.

CS8.question: What can you ask a company to tell you about your data?
options: A summary of your data, what it does with it, and who it shared it with
A copy of everything, ready to move to another app
CS8.explanation: You have a right to that summary, including who else got your data. India's law doesn't give you a portable copy.

LS9.question: What does s. 11(1) entitle Meera to?
shortAnswerOptions: A summary of her data and its processing, and the identities of everyone it was shared with
A portable copy of all her data
LS9.modelAnswer: s. 11(1)(a) gives a summary of the personal data processed and the processing activities; s. 11(1)(b) the identities of all other Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors it was shared with, with a description of the data shared; s. 11(1)(c) any other prescribed information. There is no right to data portability, unlike GDPR Art. 20. Under s. 11(2), clauses (b) and (c) don't cover sharing with another Data Fiduciary authorised by law to obtain the data, on its written request, for preventing, detecting or investigating offences or cyber incidents, or for prosecuting or punishing offences.

CS9.question: BazaarBox keeps Meera's invoices after she asks it to erase her data. Is that allowed?
options: Yes, if another law requires it to keep them
CS9.explanation: Companies must erase your data when asked, except what a law requires them to keep.

LS10.question: BazaarBox erased Meera's profile but kept her invoices and order records. Is that lawful?
LS10.modelAnswer: Yes. s. 12(3) requires erasure on request unless retention is necessary for the specified purpose or for compliance with law; s. 8(7) says the same, and its Illustration (II) gives a bank keeping identity records because banking law requires it. Rule 8(3) also requires personal data and processing logs to be kept for at least one year for the purposes in the Seventh Schedule; its Illustration (Case 1) has an e-book platform keeping order details for a year even after the user deletes her account. Under s. 8(7)(b) BazaarBox must also have its Data Processors erase data it gave them. A complaint about lawful retention risks breaching the s. 15(d) duty not to file false or frivolous complaints.

CS10.question: A big shopping app must erase your data if you haven't used it for:
CS10.explanation: For shopping apps with at least 2 crore users, it's three years of inactivity, and they must warn you 48 hours before.

LS11.question: Meera stopped using BazaarBox a year ago. Does Rule 8 already require BazaarBox to erase her data?
LS11.modelAnswer: No. Rule 8(1) and Third Schedule item 1 apply to e-commerce entities with at least 2 crore registered users in India. They must erase data (except what's needed for account access or virtual tokens) three years after the latest of: when she last approached the fiduciary for the specified purpose or exercised her rights, or the commencement of the Rules. One year is not enough, and her access request in Scene 3 counts as exercising her rights, which restarts the period. Rule 8(2) requires a warning at least 48 hours before erasure. This gives effect to s. 8(7)(a) and s. 8(8).

CF8.title: Asking what they know
CF8.plain: You can ask a company for a summary of your data, what it does with it, and who it shared it with. You don't get a portable copy.

CF9.title: Fix it or delete it
CF9.plain: You can ask a company to correct, complete or update your data, or to erase it.

CF10.title: When they can keep it
CF10.plain: A company can keep data a law requires it to keep, like tax records, and must keep order records for at least a year. It must have its processors erase what it gave them.

CF11.title: Company first, Board second
CF11.plain: Complain to the company first. If it doesn't fix the problem, you can go to the Data Protection Board.

CF12.title: The three-year rule
CF12.plain: Big shopping, gaming and social media apps must erase the data of users inactive for three years, with 48 hours' warning.

CF13.title: Who to contact
CF13.plain: Every company must publish who answers your data questions, and name that person in its replies.
CF13.law: s. 8(9); Rule 9; for Significant Data Fiduciaries, a Data Protection Officer based in India (s. 10(2)(a))
